title: Endless SQL
subtitle: Drill SQL concepts from basic filtering and joins to aggregates, conditional logic, and window functions. Real Postgres (PGlite WASM), running entirely in your browser.

exercises.title: High earners
exercises.question: Return the **first name** and **salary** of every employee who earns more than 70,000, highest salary first.
exercises.hint: WHERE filters rows before they come back; ORDER BY ... DESC sorts from highest to lowest.
exercises.solution:
SELECT first_name, salary
FROM employees
WHERE salary > 70000
ORDER BY salary DESC;

exercises.title: Salary range with BETWEEN
exercises.question: Return the **first_name**, **last_name**, and **salary** of all employees whose salary is between **50,000 and 70,000** (inclusive). Order by salary ascending.
exercises.hint: Use WHERE salary BETWEEN 50000 AND 70000 ORDER BY salary ASC.
exercises.solution:
SELECT first_name, last_name, salary
FROM employees
WHERE salary BETWEEN 50000 AND 70000
ORDER BY salary ASC;

exercises.title: Recent hires
exercises.question: Return the **first_name**, **last_name**, and **hired_at** date of all employees hired on or after **2022-01-01**, ordered by hire date ascending.
exercises.hint: Use WHERE hired_at >= '2022-01-01' and ORDER BY hired_at ASC.
exercises.solution:
SELECT first_name, last_name, hired_at
FROM employees
WHERE hired_at >= '2022-01-01'
ORDER BY hired_at ASC;

exercises.title: Pattern matching with LIKE
exercises.question: Return the **first_name** and **last_name** of all employees whose last name starts with **'K'** or **'W'**, ordered by last name ascending.
exercises.hint: Use LIKE 'K%' OR LIKE 'W%' in your WHERE clause.
exercises.solution:
SELECT first_name, last_name
FROM employees
WHERE last_name LIKE 'K%' OR last_name LIKE 'W%'
ORDER BY last_name ASC;

exercises.title: Full employee names
exercises.question: Return a single column **full_name** combining `first_name` and `last_name` separated by a space (e.g. 'Ava Chen'), along with their **salary**. Order by salary descending.
exercises.hint: In SQL, concatenate strings using the || operator: first_name || ' ' || last_name AS full_name.

exercises.title: Hiring year extraction
exercises.question: For each employee, extract the year they were hired as an integer column named **hire_year**. Return **first_name**, **last_name**, and **hire_year**, ordered by hire_year ascending, then first_name ascending.
exercises.hint: Use EXTRACT(YEAR FROM hired_at)::INTEGER AS hire_year.
exercises.solution:
SELECT first_name, last_name,
       EXTRACT(YEAR FROM hired_at)::INTEGER AS hire_year
FROM employees
ORDER BY hire_year ASC, first_name ASC;

exercises.title: Projected 10% raise
exercises.question: Calculate a 10% salary raise for all Engineering employees (`department_id = 1`). Return **first_name**, current **salary**, and the projected salary rounded to an integer aliased as **new_salary**. Order by new_salary descending.
exercises.hint: Multiply salary by 1.10 and wrap in ROUND(...)::INTEGER AS new_salary.
exercises.solution:
SELECT first_name, salary,
       ROUND(salary * 1.10)::INTEGER AS new_salary
FROM employees
WHERE department_id = 1
ORDER BY new_salary DESC;

exercises.title: Who sits where
exercises.question: Every employee's **first name**, **last name**, and **department name** (aliased as `department`) — one row per employee who has a department, ordered alphabetically by last name.
exercises.hint: employees has department_id, departments has the names. JOIN on it, and alias the department column so the header reads department.
exercises.solution:
SELECT e.first_name, e.last_name, d.name AS department
FROM employees e
JOIN departments d ON e.department_id = d.id
ORDER BY e.last_name ASC;

exercises.title: Department fallback with COALESCE
exercises.question: Return each employee's **first_name**, **last_name**, and their department name aliased as **department**. If an employee has no department (`NULL`), display `'Unassigned'` instead. Order by first_name ascending.
exercises.hint: Use a LEFT JOIN from employees to departments, and wrap d.name in COALESCE(d.name, 'Unassigned') AS department.
exercises.solution:
SELECT e.first_name, e.last_name,
       COALESCE(d.name, 'Unassigned') AS department
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN departments d ON e.department_id = d.id
ORDER BY e.first_name ASC;

exercises.title: Unassigned employees (NULLs)
exercises.question: Return the **first_name**, **last_name**, and **salary** of any employee who does **not** belong to any department (`department_id IS NULL`). Order by salary descending.
exercises.hint: Use IS NULL to filter columns that have missing/null values.
exercises.solution:
SELECT first_name, last_name, salary
FROM employees
WHERE department_id IS NULL
ORDER BY salary DESC;

exercises.title: Department headcount
exercises.question: For each department, return its **name** (aliased as `department`), the **number of employees** (aliased as `employee_count`), and the **average salary** (aliased as `avg_salary`) rounded to 2 decimals. Order by department name.
exercises.hint: GROUP BY collapses rows per group; COUNT(*) counts them and AVG() averages the salary. ROUND(avg, 2) cleans up the decimals.
exercises.solution:
SELECT d.name AS department,
       COUNT(*) AS employee_count,
       ROUND(AVG(e.salary), 2) AS avg_salary
FROM employees e
JOIN departments d ON e.department_id = d.id
GROUP BY d.name
ORDER BY d.name ASC;

exercises.title: Well-paid teams
exercises.question: Which departments have an **average salary above 70,000**? Return the department **name** (aliased as `department`) and its **average salary** (aliased as `avg_salary`) rounded to 2 decimals, ordered by department name.
exercises.hint: You can't filter an aggregate with WHERE — that's what HAVING is for. The aggregate has to be repeated in HAVING, not aliased.
exercises.solution:
SELECT d.name AS department,
       ROUND(AVG(e.salary), 2) AS avg_salary
FROM employees e
JOIN departments d ON e.department_id = d.id
GROUP BY d.name
HAVING AVG(e.salary) > 70000
ORDER BY d.name ASC;

exercises.title: Departments with no employees
exercises.question: Find any department that currently has **no employees assigned to it**. Return the department **name** (aliased as `department`). Order by department name ascending.
exercises.hint: Use a LEFT JOIN from departments to employees and filter WHERE e.id IS NULL.
exercises.solution:
SELECT d.name AS department
FROM departments d
LEFT JOIN employees e ON d.id = e.department_id
WHERE e.id IS NULL
ORDER BY d.name ASC;

exercises.title: High earner count per department
exercises.question: For each department, return its **name** (aliased as `department`), the total number of employees (aliased as `total_employees`), and the count of employees earning **over 70,000** (aliased as `high_earners_count`). Order by department name ascending.
exercises.hint: Use conditional aggregation: COUNT(CASE WHEN e.salary > 70000 THEN 1 END) AS high_earners_count.
exercises.solution:
SELECT d.name AS department,
       COUNT(e.id) AS total_employees,
       COUNT(CASE WHEN e.salary > 70000 THEN 1 END) AS high_earners_count
FROM departments d
LEFT JOIN employees e ON d.id = e.department_id
GROUP BY d.name
ORDER BY d.name ASC;

exercises.title: Salary bands (CASE WHEN)
exercises.question: Categorize employees into salary bands: **'High'** (salary >= 80000), **'Medium'** (salary BETWEEN 60000 AND 79999), and **'Entry'** (salary < 60000). Return **first_name**, **salary**, and the band (aliased as `salary_band`), ordered by salary descending.
exercises.hint: Use CASE WHEN salary >= 80000 THEN 'High' WHEN salary >= 60000 THEN 'Medium' ELSE 'Entry' END AS salary_band.
exercises.solution:
SELECT first_name, salary,
       CASE
         WHEN salary >= 80000 THEN 'High'
         WHEN salary >= 60000 THEN 'Medium'
         ELSE 'Entry'
       END AS salary_band
FROM employees
ORDER BY salary DESC;

exercises.title: Multi-project contributors
exercises.question: Find all employees assigned to **2 or more projects**. Return their **first_name**, **last_name**, and the count of assigned projects (aliased as `project_count`), ordered by project_count descending, then last_name ascending.
exercises.hint: JOIN employees to employee_projects, GROUP BY employee columns, and filter using HAVING COUNT(ep.project_id) >= 2.
exercises.solution:
SELECT e.first_name, e.last_name,
       COUNT(ep.project_id) AS project_count
FROM employees e
JOIN employee_projects ep ON e.id = ep.employee_id
GROUP BY e.id, e.first_name, e.last_name
HAVING COUNT(ep.project_id) >= 2
ORDER BY project_count DESC, e.last_name ASC;

exercises.title: Above average earners
exercises.question: Return the **first_name**, **last_name**, and **salary** of all employees who earn **strictly more than the overall company average salary**. Order by salary descending.
exercises.hint: Use a subquery in your WHERE clause: WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees).
exercises.solution:
SELECT first_name, last_name, salary
FROM employees
WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees)
ORDER BY salary DESC;

exercises.title: Department payroll comparison
exercises.question: Using a CTE, calculate each department's total payroll (`total_payroll`). Return department **name** (aliased as `department`) and **total_payroll** for departments where total payroll exceeds 120,000, ordered by total_payroll descending.
exercises.hint: Use WITH dept_payroll AS (SELECT d.name AS department, SUM(e.salary) AS total_payroll ... GROUP BY d.name) SELECT department, total_payroll FROM dept_payroll WHERE total_payroll > 120000 ORDER BY total_payroll DESC.
exercises.solution:
WITH dept_payroll AS (
  SELECT d.name AS department, SUM(e.salary) AS total_payroll
  FROM employees e
  JOIN departments d ON e.department_id = d.id
  GROUP BY d.name
)
SELECT department, total_payroll
FROM dept_payroll
WHERE total_payroll > 120000
ORDER BY total_payroll DESC;

exercises.title: Top earners per team
exercises.question: Return the **top 2 earners in each department**: department name (aliased as `department`), first name, last name, and salary. Order by department name, then salary descending.
exercises.hint: DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY salary DESC) numbers rows within each department without eliminating them — rank in a CTE, then filter the rank in the outer query.
exercises.solution:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT d.name AS department,
         e.first_name,
         e.last_name,
         e.salary,
         DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY d.name ORDER BY e.salary DESC) AS rnk
  FROM employees e
  JOIN departments d ON e.department_id = d.id
)
SELECT department, first_name, last_name, salary
FROM ranked
WHERE rnk <= 2
ORDER BY department ASC, salary DESC;

exercises.title: Running total payroll
exercises.question: Calculate a cumulative running total of employee salaries in order of their `hired_at` date. Return **first_name**, **hired_at**, **salary**, and the cumulative total (aliased as `running_total`), ordered by `hired_at` ascending, then `id` ascending.
exercises.hint: Use SUM(salary) OVER (ORDER BY hired_at ASC, id ASC) AS running_total.
exercises.solution:
SELECT first_name, hired_at, salary,
       SUM(salary) OVER (ORDER BY hired_at ASC, id ASC) AS running_total
FROM employees
ORDER BY hired_at ASC, id ASC;

exercises.title: Previous hire salary (LAG)
exercises.question: For each employee, find the salary of the employee hired immediately before them. Return **first_name**, **hired_at**, **salary**, and the previous hire's salary (aliased as `prev_salary`), ordered by `hired_at` ascending, then `id` ascending.
exercises.hint: Use LAG(salary) OVER (ORDER BY hired_at ASC, id ASC) AS prev_salary.
exercises.solution:
SELECT first_name, hired_at, salary,
       LAG(salary) OVER (ORDER BY hired_at ASC, id ASC) AS prev_salary
FROM employees
ORDER BY hired_at ASC, id ASC;

exercises.title: Project budget allocation
exercises.question: For each employee assigned to a project, return their **first_name**, **last_name**, project name (aliased as `project_name`), and project **budget**. Order by project budget descending, then employee last name ascending.
exercises.hint: Join employees to employee_projects, and employee_projects to projects. Alias p.name AS project_name.
exercises.solution:
SELECT e.first_name, e.last_name, p.name AS project_name, p.budget
FROM employees e
JOIN employee_projects ep ON e.id = ep.employee_id
JOIN projects p ON ep.project_id = p.id
ORDER BY p.budget DESC, e.last_name ASC;
